If credits are property, the registry must repay clients for any credits lost in the insolvency.
If credits are property, they can be held on trust and kept outside the custodian's insolvent estate.
If credits are contractual rights, the liquidator must retire them for the clients' benefit first.
rationales: Clients usually do not hold the registry account themselves; the custodian does. That is why their position is uncertain today.
Registries do not guarantee title or compensate holders. Protection comes from trust structures, not registry payouts.

Correct. As property, credits can be held on trust and kept separate from the custodian's own assets, so clients are protected if it fails. As mere contractual rights, clients may be left with only a claim against the custodian.
No such rule exists. Without property status, clients may simply be unsecured creditors.
questions.takeaway: Property status lets custodians hold credits on trust, protecting clients in insolvency.

questions.stem: Insurers today offer cover for non-delivery and political risk on carbon deals, but struggle to offer title insurance on the credits themselves. Why?
options: Registries already guarantee title to credits, so separate title cover would duplicate what buyers have.
Title insurance is banned for intangible assets, so insurers can only ever cover a project's physical assets.
Insurers can only pay claims in replacement credits, which makes any title cover impossible to settle.
Today's cover sits behind a contract with a chosen law; insuring title needs credits to be treated as property.
rationales: Registries do not guarantee title. That gap is part of the problem.
Nothing bans title insurance for intangible assets. The obstacle is the credit's unclear legal nature.
Many policies pay in cash. Settlement in replacement credits is an option, not a limit on insuring title.

Correct. Insurance works today because the policy sits behind a contract with a chosen governing law: you insure the deal, not the credit. If credits were property, cover for title, loss or impairment would become possible.
questions.takeaway: Today you insure the deal; if credits become property, you can insure the credit itself.

questions.stem: Which initiative's 2024 final report concluded that legal uncertainty is holding back the VCM, yet chose not to prescribe a definition of carbon credits?
options: HCCH, which convened an experts' group on cross-border issues, starting with the applicable-law rule.
IOSCO, which asked each jurisdiction to clarify the legal nature and regulatory status of credits.
ISDA, which reviewed France, Japan and Singapore and found credits are, or should be, intangible property.
UNIDROIT, which drafted principles recognising credits as intangible assets open to proprietary rights.
rationales: The Hague Conference's experts' group (2025) works on cross-border, private international law issues, not a general report on legal uncertainty.

Correct. IOSCO's 2024 Final Report found that legal uncertainty is holding back the VCM. It prescribed no definition but said each jurisdiction should clarify the legal nature and regulatory classification of credits.
ISDA's 2022 paper took a view on property status in three jurisdictions. It is not the 2024 report described here.
UNIDROIT did take a position: its draft Principles treat credits as intangible assets that can be subject to proprietary rights.
questions.takeaway: UNIDROIT drafts principles; ISDA reviews jurisdictions; IOSCO urges clarity; HCCH tackles cross-border law.

questions.stem: A Singapore SME wants to retire a few hundred credits from Verra and Gold Standard projects for its annual report, with as little administration as possible. What is the most suitable route?
options: Open Verra and Gold Standard registry accounts, buy spot on an exchange, then retire the credits itself.
Sign a primary ERPA with each developer to secure forward delivery into its own registry accounts.
Join a buyer alliance such as Frontier, which pools small buyers and retires credits on their behalf.
Buy through a platform or service provider that retires the credits for it, without taking delivery.
rationales: This works but adds cost and administration: separate registry accounts, each with its own interface, terms and fees, plus exchange access. It is overkill for a few hundred credits.
Primary ERPAs are wholesale, bespoke forward contracts with developers, which is far beyond what a small one-off retirement needs.
Frontier is an advance market commitment for carbon removals that aggregates large buyers' demand. It is not a retail retirement service.
Correct. For small volumes bought to retire, platforms and service providers offer curation, due diligence and retirement. Buying this way means the company does not have to take delivery.
questions.takeaway: Small buyers who only want to retire credits can use platforms and avoid taking delivery.

questions.stem: A trading firm wants to hold Verra VCUs and Gold Standard credits in its own name so that it can resell them. What must it do?
options: Open no account at all, since resale only needs a contract that lists the credits' serial numbers.
Open one account at any registry, since registries are linked and credits move freely between all of them.
Open an exchange account only, since exchanges hold credits for members without involving a registry.
Open an account at each registry, since credits are delivered by transfer between accounts in that registry.
rationales: A contract can transfer the economic interest, but holding credits in its own name requires a registry account.
Registries are not interchangeable. If you want Verra credits you need a Verra account, and if you want Gold Standard credits you need a Gold Standard account.
Exchanges facilitate trading, but delivery still settles into registry accounts.

Correct. Credits are stored in a registry and delivered by electronic transfer between accounts in it. To hold credits from different standards, a company must open multiple registry accounts, each with its own interface, terms and fees.
questions.takeaway: Taking delivery means opening a registry account with each standard you want to hold.

questions.stem: A tech company wants the lowest-cost access to credits and strong control over their quality. It has in-house expertise and can accept long lead times and the risk that a methodology is rejected. Which transaction type fits best?
options: A forward offtake agreement, paying on later delivery to hedge itself against price volatility.
A spot purchase direct from a developer, avoiding broker fees and any long-term commitment.
A project investment, entering at origination for control over quality and low-cost access.
A spot purchase via an exchange, gaining immediate access to a liquid and broad product range.
rationales: Offtakes give cheaper access and a hedge, but less control and involvement than investing directly in the project.
Spot purchases from developers avoid commitment but offer little control over quality, and unsold stock may raise quality concerns.

Correct. In the MSCI framework, investing in a project, especially one developing a new methodology, offers competitive advantage, strong control over quality and the lowest-cost access. In return it needs expertise, accepts long lead times and carries the risk that the methodology is rejected.
Exchange spot buying gives liquidity and immediacy, but costs more and offers no control over the project.
questions.takeaway: Further upstream means more control and lower cost, but more expertise needed and more risk.

questions.stem: A buyer pays US$5 million in 2026 for credits to be delivered between 2028 and 2030. What type of transaction is this, and what is its key exposure?
options: A pre-purchase agreement, exposing the buyer to non-delivery since it pays before any credits are issued.
A spot transaction, exposing the buyer to quality risk since the developer's stock may be unsold for a reason.
A forward agreement, exposing the buyer to price risk since it pays the market price on each delivery.
A project investment, exposing the buyer to methodology risk since it funds a new crediting approach.
rationales: Correct. Paying now and receiving later is a pre-purchase. The buyer commits capital up front, and delivery is not certain.
Spot means immediate delivery of existing credits. Here delivery comes years later.
A forward agreement means paying later on delivery, usually at a pre-agreed price. Here payment is up front.
The buyer is purchasing future credits, not taking an equity stake or funding the development of a methodology.
questions.takeaway: Pre-purchase: pay now, receive later. Forward: pay later, receive later. Both carry delivery risk.

questions.stem: Project X fails to deliver the credits it promised forward buyers. Why can't the developer simply buy 'equivalent' credits from Project Y at a single market price to make good?
options: Credits from other projects carry no serial numbers, so their delivery cannot be confirmed on a registry.
Credits can be delivered only from the project named in the ERPA, since substituting them is legally barred.
Credits from other projects must be retired immediately, so they cannot be transferred to another buyer.
Credits differ by registry, methodology and jurisdiction, so few are true substitutes at a single price.
rationales: Every issued credit carries a serial number, so delivery can always be confirmed.
ERPAs often include replacement clauses, so substitution is not barred. It is just hard to find a true equivalent.
Issued credits can be transferred before retirement. Nothing forces immediate retirement.
Correct. VCM pricing is fragmented across registries, methodologies and jurisdictions, with no single price. That fragmentation makes substitution hard and keeps deep pools of liquidity from forming.
questions.takeaway: Fragmented pricing makes credits poor substitutes for one another and limits liquidity.

questions.stem: A buyer chooses to trade on an exchange rather than over the counter, even though exchange contracts cannot be tailored. What is the main advantage it gains?
options: Exchange contracts name a single specific project, so the buyer knows exactly which credits it will get.
Central clearing removes its exposure to the counterparty's performance, and terms need no negotiation.
Exchange prices include a corresponding adjustment, so the credits are automatically eligible for CORSIA.
The exchange guarantees the quality of every credit, so the buyer no longer needs to do due diligence.
rationales: Exchange contracts are usually standardised across many projects, often on a cheapest-to-deliver basis, so the buyer may not know which project it will receive.

Correct. In the classical exchange model, central clearing removes exposure to the counterparty's performance, with implications for KYC, credit risk and delivery risk. Standardisation removes the need to negotiate each deal.
Corresponding adjustments depend on host-country authorisation, not on the trading venue. Some contracts do target CORSIA units, but the venue itself does not confer eligibility.
Standardised criteria set a minimum bar, but exchanges do not guarantee each credit's quality.
questions.takeaway: Exchanges offer central clearing and standardisation; OTC offers customisation.

questions.stem: A buyer goes long a CIX Nature X contract, under which credits from eleven different REDD+ projects can be delivered. Which credits is it most likely to receive?
options: Whichever eligible credits are cheapest for the seller, since the seller decides what to deliver.
Whichever eligible credits the buyer nominates, since the buyer chooses at the time of settlement.
An equal mix of all eligible projects, since the exchange pro-rates delivery across the basket.
The highest-rated eligible credits, since the exchange ranks deliverable projects by integrity.
rationales: Correct. Under cheapest-to-deliver, any eligible credit satisfies the contract, so the seller delivers the lowest-cost one. That is why the price spread within the basket should not be too wide.
The buyer does not choose. That optionality sits with the seller.
Delivery is not pro-rated across the basket. The seller picks.
Exchanges set eligibility criteria but do not rank projects for delivery.
questions.takeaway: Standardised contracts are typically cheapest-to-deliver: the seller delivers the lowest-cost eligible credit.

questions.stem: Why do exchanges list standardised contracts, such as 'nature-based, Southeast Asia, issued after 2019', rather than contracts for individual projects?
options: To pool supply from many projects into one contract, deepening liquidity and aiding price risk management.
To raise credit quality, since registries issue credits only to projects that meet every listed criterion.
To guarantee corresponding adjustments, since standardised contracts accept only authorised units.
To avoid KYC obligations, since standardised contracts do not need to identify either buyer or seller.
rationales: Correct. Standardisation lets liquidity concentrate, bringing greater fungibility, more room for substitution and better price risk management. It also guards against manipulation and price dislocations.
Registries issue credits under their own standards, not under exchange contract criteria. The criteria only define what can be delivered.
Authorisation is a separate matter. Most standardised contracts are not built around corresponding adjustments.
KYC requirements still apply. Clearing changes who bears the risk; it does not remove identification.
questions.takeaway: Standardised contracts pool liquidity, aid substitution and support price discovery.

questions.stem: A buyer and a developer negotiating an IETA primary ERPA want the right to reprice or exit if Verra revises the methodology the project relies on. Which clause best achieves this?
options: A change-in-law clause defined to cover changes to the carbon standard's rules, not just legislation.
A delivery-window clause, which allows for registry delays before either party can declare a default.
A pay-on-delivery clause, which holds the buyer's payment in escrow until the credits are transferred.
A price-floor clause, which fixes a minimum price whatever happens to the market or to the methodology.
rationales: Correct. A carbon-specific feature of ERPAs is that 'change of law' includes changes to the rules of the carbon standard, such as Verra's. Such a clause lets the parties reprice or exit if those rules change.
Delivery windows handle registry and verification delays. They do not handle a permanent cut in issuance.
Escrow protects against counterparty default. It does not adjust terms when the rules change.
A price floor addresses price risk and would not give either party an exit if the methodology changes.
questions.takeaway: ERPAs define 'change of law' to include changes to the carbon standard's rules.

questions.stem: A group of tech firms wants to speed up nascent carbon removal technologies that cannot yet deliver at scale. Which purchasing approach best fits this aim?
options: A standardised futures contract, letting buyers hedge prices on removals already being issued.
A retail marketplace purchase, which curates and retires small volumes on each firm's behalf.
An advance market commitment that pools buyers' demand and contracts mainly on a forward basis.
A spot purchase on an exchange, giving immediate delivery from a broad range of existing projects.
rationales: Futures depend on liquid, standardised supply, which early-stage removals do not have.
Retail marketplaces suit small retirements, not building demand for new technology.
Correct. Frontier is an advance market commitment for removals. It aggregates demand, runs regular RFPs and relies mostly on forward contracts, given how early-stage the technology is.
Spot buying needs credits that already exist. Nascent removals cannot yet supply them at scale.
questions.takeaway: Buyer alliances such as Frontier pool demand and buy forward to help nascent removals scale.

questions.stem: In its carbon removal RFPs, Microsoft requires suppliers to take on obligations if stored CO2 is released, to maintain a buffer and to notify it of reversals. What makes this possible?
options: It buys CORSIA units, for which ICAO requires suppliers to hold a buffer and to notify reversals.
Its RFPs follow IETA's template, which requires these terms in every purchase of carbon removals.
It buys only on exchanges, whose rulebooks impose these obligations on every supplier of credits.
Its scale gives it leverage to set bespoke terms, such as reversal duties, buffers and notice.
rationales: Microsoft's removals are voluntary purchases, not CORSIA compliance units.
IETA templates exist, but resourceful firms can draft their own. These terms come from Microsoft's own negotiation.
Microsoft's RFPs are bilateral procurement, not exchange trades.
Correct. Larger organisations may have the capacity and leverage to negotiate bespoke provisions. Microsoft's terms on reversal, buffers and notification are an example.
questions.takeaway: Large buyers can use RFPs to impose bespoke protections such as reversal and buffer obligations.

questions.stem: Which description best matches how carbon credits are mostly transacted today?
options: Mostly through buyer alliances, which have replaced bilateral deals for most large-volume purchases.
Mostly on exchanges, where standardised contracts now provide deep liquidity across most credit types.
Mostly OTC or hybrid investment deals, with forwards and pre-purchases a big share of offtake.
Mostly through retail platforms, which now account for the bulk of credits retired by large companies.
rationales: Buyer alliances such as Frontier matter for removals, but bilateral OTC deals still dominate.
Exchange-based instruments exist, but liquidity is limited to pockets.

Correct. Most transactions today are OTC trades or hybrid investment and streaming deals. In 2025, offtake overtook investment, and forwards and pre-purchases made up about two-thirds of offtake value.
Retail platforms serve small buyers. They are not the bulk of the market.
questions.takeaway: The market is mostly OTC and forward offtake; exchange liquidity remains thin.

questions.stem: In 2023 Verra inactivated a rice cultivation methodology, and in 2024 it rejected 37 projects in China that had already issued millions of credits. Which risk does this illustrate?
options: Invalidation risk, as credits or projects were rejected over problems with the methodology.
Reversal risk, as carbon already credited to the projects was released back into the atmosphere.
Political risk, as the host government changed its rules on which projects could export credits.
Price risk, as the market value of rice credits fell once buyers lost confidence in the projects.
rationales: Correct. Invalidation is the risk that credits or a whole project are invalidated through negligence, fraud, significant methodology shifts or reversals. The rice case is the course's invalidation precedent.
Rice methane credits are avoidance credits. Nothing stored was released, so this is not a reversal.
The decision came from the crediting programme, not a host government.
Prices may well have fallen, but the triggering event was the programme rejecting projects and their credits.
questions.takeaway: Methodology problems leading to rejected credits are invalidation risk.

questions.stem: Between 2015 and 2021, wildfires used up nearly one-fifth of California's forest offset buffer pool, which was designed to cover 100 years of reversal risk. What limitation of buffer pools does this expose?
options: Buffer credits can be sold, so programmes run the pool down whenever market prices rise sharply.
Buffers cover only political risk, so any wildfire losses fall entirely on the credit holders instead.
Losses are correlated, so one bad stretch can drain a pool sized as if reversals were independent.
Buffers are funded by buyers' premiums, so the pool shrinks whenever buyers stop renewing cover.
rationales: Buffer credits cannot be sold. That is why buffers raise the cost per credit delivered.
Buffers exist to cover reversal, such as fire, not political risk.
Correct. A buffer is the system insuring itself. Because wildfire losses are correlated across projects, a few bad years can consume reserves meant to last a century.
Buffers are funded by projects setting aside a share of their credits, not by buyers' premiums.
questions.takeaway: Buffer pools are self-insurance and are vulnerable to correlated losses.

questions.stem: Under Verra's durability pilot, launched in December 2025, an eligible AFOLU project uses approved insurance instead of contributing credits to the pooled buffer. What is the main commercial benefit?
options: The project no longer faces reversal risk, since insurance removes the need to monitor stored carbon.
Buyers no longer need due diligence, since an insured credit is guaranteed to be of high quality.
Credits that would have sat in the buffer can be issued and sold, improving capital efficiency.
The project's credits gain CORSIA eligibility automatically, since the insurance stands in for an LoA.
rationales: Insurance transfers the financial consequence of a reversal. The physical risk and the need to monitor remain.
An insurer's willingness to cover may signal quality, but it guarantees nothing about the credit.
Correct. Buffer credits cannot be sold, which raises the cost per credit delivered. Replacing the buffer contribution with insurance releases those credits for issuance.
CORSIA eligibility still requires host-country authorisation. Insurance against a missing corresponding adjustment is a separate requirement.
questions.takeaway: Insurance in place of buffer contributions frees up credits that would otherwise be locked away.

questions.stem: A developer's risk team asks which risks good project design and contracts cannot reduce, and so must be retained or transferred, for example to an insurer. Which pair is it?
options: Counterparty risk and legal risk, which persist however carefully the developer drafts its contracts.
Operational risk and social risk, which depend on local communities the developer cannot influence.
Methodology risk and registry risk, which are set by the crediting programme rather than the developer.
Political risk and extreme weather, which sit outside the developer's control however well it designs.
rationales: Counterparty and legal risk are classed as largely mitigable through project design and contracts.
Operational and social risk are also largely mitigable. Community engagement is part of good design.
Carbon-related risks such as registry and methodology are partly mitigable, partly outside the developer's control, but not unavoidable.
Correct. In Kita's framework, political risk and extreme weather or natural catastrophe are unavoidable. They cannot be designed out, so they must be retained or transferred.
questions.takeaway: Mitigable: operational, counterparty, legal, social. Partly: ecological, carbon, regulatory. Unavoidable: political, natural catastrophe.

questions.stem: A forward buyer is worried that the developer will become insolvent after being paid but before delivering the credits. Which ERPA term most directly addresses this?
options: A replacement clause, so the developer must deliver substitute credits after any shortfall that occurs.
Index-linked pricing, so the amount paid tracks the market price at the time of each delivery.
A delivery window, so registry delays do not trigger a default before the credits are actually issued.
Pay-on-delivery or escrow terms, so the buyer's money is released only once credits are transferred.
rationales: A replacement clause depends on the developer being able to perform. An insolvent developer may not be able to deliver substitutes.
Pricing terms allocate price risk. They do not protect money already paid.
Delivery windows give the seller more time. They do not protect the buyer against insolvency.
Correct. Pay-on-delivery or escrow protects the buyer's payment until delivery. That addresses counterparty risk directly.
questions.takeaway: Escrow or pay-on-delivery addresses counterparty risk; replacement clauses still depend on the seller.

questions.stem: A forward buyer's ERPA contains a strong make-good clause. A fire destroys the project, and the developer becomes insolvent. Why may the clause give the buyer little protection?
options: Make-good clauses cover only invalidation, so a reversal caused by fire falls outside the clause's scope.
Make-good clauses need approval from the crediting programme, which is rarely given to forestry projects.
Make-good clauses are void unless credits are recognised as property under the law governing the ERPA.
A contractual remedy is only as good as the counterparty's ability to pay, and this developer cannot pay.
rationales: Replacement and make-good clauses typically cover shortfall, reversal and cancellation, so fire is within scope. Enforcing the clause is the problem.
Contract terms between buyer and seller do not need approval from the crediting programme.
Contracts are enforceable whether or not credits are property. Contracts are what the market relies on today.

Correct. A contractual remedy depends on the other party's ability to pay, and an insolvent developer may be unable to pay damages or replace credits. Such remaining risks can be transferred to a third party such as an insurer.
questions.takeaway: Contracts reallocate risk only as far as the counterparty can pay; insurance can cover the rest.

questions.stem: An ERPA contains a broad force majeure and change-of-law clause. The host government then refuses to authorise the project's credits. Who most likely ends up bearing the loss?
options: The host government, since refusing authorisation automatically triggers compensation under the ERPA.
The buyer, since the clause may excuse the seller's performance and leave the loss with the buyer.
The crediting programme, since its pooled buffer covers losses caused by refused authorisations.
The seller, since force majeure clauses protect only the party that has already received payment.
rationales: The government is not a party to the ERPA, so the contract cannot make it pay compensation.
Correct. Force majeure and change-of-law clauses may excuse the seller, which leaves the risk with the buyer. Neither party controls government decisions.
Buffers cover reversal. Political risk such as refused authorisation falls outside them.
Force majeure typically excuses the party that cannot perform, here the seller. It does not protect whoever has been paid.
questions.takeaway: Force majeure and change-of-law clauses can push political risk onto the buyer.

questions.stem: A bank has lent against a project's offtake receivables and is worried that the offtaker will not pay. Which Kita product is designed for this?
options: Political Risk Insurance, which covers investors if a host government revokes a Letter of Authorisation.
Non-Delivery Insurance, which covers buyers when forward credits are not delivered in part or in full.
Counterparty Insurance, which covers early buyers if the developer abandons the project or goes insolvent.
Non-Payment Insurance, which covers lenders against non-payment on prepayments and offtake receivables.
rationales: Political Risk Insurance covers government action. Here the risk is the offtaker's payment.
Non-Delivery covers credits that are not delivered. The bank's worry is that cash will not be paid.
Counterparty Insurance is for buyers and investors in very early-stage projects, not lenders worried about receivables.
Correct. Non-Payment Insurance is aimed at lenders and banks. It covers non-payment under project finance, prepayments and offtake receivables, which is counterparty risk.
questions.takeaway: Match the product to the risk and the insured: lenders' payment risk calls for Non-Payment Insurance.

questions.stem: A trader wants protection against a sudden collapse in nature-based credit prices, like the 37% one-day fall in December 2022. What should it be told?
options: Buffer Depletion Insurance covers price falls, since falling prices reduce the value of buffer credits.
Non-Delivery Insurance covers price falls, since claims can be paid in replacement credits instead.
Price risk is not covered by carbon insurance; it is managed through contract price terms and hedging.
Political Risk Insurance covers price falls, since prices usually fall after host-country rule changes.
rationales: Buffer Depletion Insurance is bought by carbon standards to restore a depleted buffer, which is reversal risk.
Non-Delivery covers credits that are not delivered, not a fall in their market value.
Correct. Kita's product map explicitly excludes price risk, which is managed through contract terms such as fixed, floor or index-linked pricing, and through hedging.
Political Risk Insurance covers events such as confiscation or a revoked LoA, not market price movements.
questions.takeaway: Price risk is not insured; it is handled through contract pricing and hedging.

questions.stem: An investor funds a project at concept stage, before validation, and wants cover in case the developer abandons it or becomes insolvent. Which Kita product fits, and what can happen to it at validation?
options: Non-Payment Insurance, which can convert into Non-Delivery Insurance once an offtake is signed with a buyer.
Political Risk Insurance, which can convert into Buffer Depletion Insurance once credits are issued.
Non-Delivery Insurance, which can convert into Counterparty Insurance once credits are first issued.
Counterparty Insurance, which can convert into Non-Delivery Insurance once the project is validated.
rationales: Non-Payment covers lenders' receivables. It is not the pre-validation product.
Political Risk and Buffer Depletion insure different parties against different risks, and neither converts into the other.
This reverses the conversion, which runs from Counterparty to Non-Delivery at validation.
Correct. Counterparty Insurance is designed for pre-validation projects, covering a developer that abandons the project or becomes insolvent. It can convert into Non-Delivery Insurance at validation.
questions.takeaway: Counterparty Insurance covers pre-validation projects and converts to Non-Delivery at validation.

questions.stem: Who is the insured party under Kita's Buffer Depletion Insurance?
options: Lenders, to protect the value of buffer credits that are pledged as security for project loans.
The carbon standard itself, to restore its pooled buffer if losses deplete it past a set threshold.
Forward buyers, to receive replacement credits if the buffer cannot cover a reversal on their project.
Each project developer, to replace its own contribution to the buffer if its stored carbon is lost.
rationales: Buffer credits cannot be sold or pledged. Lenders use Non-Payment Insurance.
Correct. Buffer Depletion Insurance is bought by carbon standards at pool level. It pays compensation to restore the buffer once losses pass an agreed threshold, which addresses reversal risk.
Forward buyers typically use Non-Delivery Insurance to protect their position.
Developers contribute to the buffer, but this product insures the pool as a whole, not each contribution.
questions.takeaway: Buffer Depletion Insurance protects the carbon standard's pool, not individual participants.

questions.stem: A developer plans to sell units into CORSIA's First Phase. Why does insurance matter for whether those units are eligible?
options: Airlines can claim insurance payouts as reductions, which lowers their offsetting requirements.
ICAO requires every EEU to carry non-delivery cover so that airlines are compensated for delays.
Programmes require cover against the host country failing to apply a corresponding adjustment.
Insured credits are exempt from the 2016 start-date rule, which widens the eligible supply pool.
rationales: Insurance payouts are cash or replacement credits. They are not emissions reductions an airline can claim.
No such ICAO rule exists. The insurance link concerns corresponding adjustments, not delivery delays.
Correct. For the First Phase, Gold Standard and Verra require cover against a host country failing to apply a corresponding adjustment. Approved insurance helps make those credits eligible.
Insurance does not override the start-date or vintage tests for eligible units.
questions.takeaway: For CORSIA's First Phase, programmes require insurance against a failed corresponding adjustment.

questions.stem: An insurer notices that the projects most eager to buy non-delivery cover tend to have problems it cannot see from the outside. Which challenge in pricing carbon insurance is this?
options: Moral hazard, as insured developers may take less care once their losses are covered by a policy.
Limited claims history, as most carbon policies are too new to give much loss data for pricing.
Signalling, as the market may read an insurer's willingness to provide cover as a quality mark.
Adverse selection, as buyers keenest on cover may carry risks that the insurer cannot observe.
rationales: Moral hazard concerns behaviour after cover is bought. The scenario describes hidden risk before cover is bought.
Thin loss data is a separate pricing challenge. The scenario is about who self-selects into cover.
Signalling is a real challenge, but it concerns how the market reads the insurer's decision, not who seeks cover.
Correct. Adverse selection means those who most want cover may be the ones with risks the insurer cannot observe.
questions.takeaway: Adverse selection: the riskiest projects are the keenest buyers of cover.

questions.stem: Koko Networks held a US$179.6m MIGA guarantee covering expropriation, war and civil disturbance, transfer restriction and breach of contract. Kenya then declined to authorise its credits. Why might the guarantee not respond?
options: The guarantee lapsed once credits were sold to traders, since cover ends when credits change hands.
Declining to authorise may be a lawful use of discretion, not a breach of contract or expropriation.
The guarantee covered traders' credits rather than Koko's investment, so Koko had no claim to make.
MIGA covers only war and civil disturbance, so any government decision falls outside the guarantee.
rationales: The guarantee covered Koko's investment for up to 15 years and was not tied to who held the credits.

Correct. Whether the refusal breached the unpublished 2024 Investment Framework Agreement is an open question. A breach-of-contract guarantee may not respond if the government was exercising a lawful discretion. Cover is limited to the policy's terms.
It was the reverse: MIGA covered Koko's investment in its Kenyan subsidiary, and the traders had no cover.
The guarantee also covered expropriation, transfer restriction and breach of contract. The question is whether this event fits any of them.
questions.takeaway: Insurance cover is limited to its terms; a lawful refusal to authorise may fall outside it.

questions.stem: Through 2025, traders bought Koko credits at around US$12 each, expecting a Letter of Authorisation that never came. Which statement best describes their position?
options: They bought before authorisation, holding uninsured political risk, and so they bore the loss.
They held CORSIA-eligible units, so the loss fell on the airlines that had planned to cancel them.
They could claim against the registry, since ICAO holds registries liable when an LoA is refused.
They were covered by MIGA's guarantee, so their loss passed to the World Bank Group's insurance arm.
rationales: Correct. Buying credits before authorisation exposed the traders to political risk. Much of the loss was uninsured, and the traders had no cover.
Without an LoA, and so without a corresponding adjustment, the credits were never CORSIA-eligible.
Registry liability concerns a host country revoking an LoA that was granted for eligible units. Here no LoA was ever issued.
MIGA's guarantee covered Koko's investment, not the traders' credits.
questions.takeaway: Buying before authorisation means holding uninsured political risk, as the Koko traders found.

questions.stem: A crediting programme revises the REDD+ methodology a project relies on, cutting the credits it can expect to issue. How does this affect the forward buyer, as distinct from the other parties?
options: Nothing changes for it, since forward contracts lock in volumes regardless of later rule changes.
Its contracted volumes may fall short, and replacement credits may cost more than it agreed to pay.
Confidence in other projects using the methodology, and in the buffer pool, may be weakened.
Money it already spent on project design and validation now produces fewer credits than planned.
rationales: Contracts cannot create credits that the methodology no longer supports. Change-of-law clauses may even excuse the seller.
Correct. For the forward buyer, contracted volumes are not delivered in full, and replacement credits may cost more.
That is the effect on the crediting programme and its other projects.
That is the developer's loss: its sunk costs now produce fewer credits.
questions.takeaway: The same event hits the developer, the forward buyer and the crediting programme differently.

questions.stem: A buyer purchases issued credits spot and holds them for three years before retiring them. Which risks does it carry while holding them?
options: Counterparty risk alone, which peaks after issuance and lasts until the credits are retired.
Reversal, invalidation and price risk, which stay with whoever holds credits after issuance.
No material risk, since issued credits are fixed on the registry and can no longer change.
Non-delivery and political risk, which are highest for whoever holds credits after issuance.
rationales: Counterparty risk peaks around issuance and is largely settled once a spot trade completes.
Correct. After issuance, reversal and invalidation risks remain with the holder, and price exposure keeps growing.
Issued credits can still be invalidated or affected by reversals, and their market value can change.
Non-delivery and political risk are highest before validation, not after issuance.
questions.takeaway: Buying issued credits costs more and carries less risk, but reversal, invalidation and price risk remain.

questions.stem: A buyer signs a forward contract for credits from a project that has not yet been validated. At this stage of the lifecycle, which risks are highest?
options: Counterparty risk alone, which peaks before validation and then falls away once the deal is signed.
Reversal and invalidation risk, which are at their highest before the project has been validated.
Non-delivery and political risk, which are at their highest before the project has been validated.
Price risk alone, since the buyer has fixed its volumes but not the price it will pay on delivery.
rationales: Counterparty risk peaks around issuance, not before validation, and signing a contract does not remove it.
Reversal and invalidation stay with the holder after issuance. They are not at their peak before validation.
Correct. Before validation, non-delivery and political risk are highest. Buying early is cheaper and gives more influence, but exposes the buyer to more risk.
Forward contracts usually fix the price in advance, and price exposure grows over the lifecycle rather than peaking early.
questions.takeaway: Before validation: non-delivery and political risk peak. Around issuance: counterparty risk. After: reversal, invalidation, price.

questions.stem: Compared with buying credits that have already been issued, buying early in a project's lifecycle typically:
options: Costs more but removes reversal risk, since credits bought early are drawn from the buffer pool.
Costs more and gives less influence, but fixes the price and removes the buyer's price exposure.
Costs less and carries less risk, since the developer bears all losses until credits are issued.
Costs less and gives more influence over the project, but leaves the buyer exposed to more risks.
rationales: Early buying is typically cheaper, and buffer credits are never sold to buyers.
This reverses both cost and influence. Early buyers typically pay less and have more say.
Early buyers carry more risk, not less. Losses before issuance can fall on them, for example through non-delivery.
Correct. Buying early is usually cheaper and gives the buyer more influence over the project, but exposes it to more risks.
questions.takeaway: Exposure depends on when you buy: earlier means cheaper and more influence, but more risk.

questions.stem: A developer in a country with an unstable government wants to protect its project against confiscation and a revoked Letter of Authorisation. Which product, and which kind of risk is it?
options: Political Risk Insurance, covering confiscation, export bans and revoked LoAs, paid out in cash.
Non-Delivery Insurance, covering natural catastrophe, fraud and negligence, paid in replacement credits.
Buffer Depletion Insurance, covering a buffer depleted past a threshold, paid to restore the pool.
Counterparty Insurance, covering developer abandonment or insolvency before the project is validated.
rationales: Correct. Political Risk Insurance covers confiscation, export bans, revoked carbon rights, a revoked LoA or corresponding adjustment, political violence and forced abandonment. It is aimed at developers, investors and lenders.
Non-Delivery Insurance is primarily for buyers and investors and covers shortfalls from catastrophe, fraud and negligence. Government action is political risk.
Buffer Depletion Insurance is bought by carbon standards for reversal risk.
Counterparty Insurance covers the developer's own failure. Here the risk comes from the government.
questions.takeaway: Developers facing host-government risk use Political Risk Insurance.
